title: GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers Deterministic Linear-Time Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm
whyItMatters: Settles the classic deterministic linear-time Minimum Spanning Tree problem—the first improvement since Chazelle (JACM 2000)—with the core algorithmic ideas generated by GPT-6.2 Astra and verified by NYU & Harvard theorists.
summary: Sanjeev Khanna (NYU Courant), Aaron Putterman (Harvard SEAS), and Junkai Song (NYU Courant) posted arXiv:2611.31187 / ECCC TR26-339 establishing a deterministic O(m)-time comparison-based algorithm for the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) problem, breaking Bernard Chazelle’s 26-year-old O(m α(m, n)) record (JACM 2000) and matching Karger–Klein–Tarjan’s 1995 randomized linear-time bound deterministically. By proving that the deterministic comparison complexity of MST is O(m) via a novel recursive edge-filtering certificate procedure and schedule-counting argument, Pettie and Ramachandran’s 2002 reduction immediately yields a deterministic linear-time pointer-machine algorithm. In Section 1.4 ('AI Acknowledgments'), the authors transparently credit OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra with generating the paper’s main ideas with minimal human intellectual intervention before the authors verified, checked, and simplified the full proof.
technicalHighlights: Proves deterministic comparison complexity T*(m, n) = O(m) for Minimum Spanning Forest, yielding a deterministic linear-time MST algorithm via Pettie–Ramachandran (JACM 2002).
Provides the first deterministic asymptotic breakthrough since Chazelle’s soft-heap O(m α(m, n)) bound in 2000 and derandomizes the 1995 Karger–Klein–Tarjan linear-time milestone.

Section 1.4 explicitly credits GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra/Max effort) with generating the core algorithmic ideas with minimal human intellectual intervention, subsequently verified and simplified by Khanna, Putterman, and Song.
caveats: Unrefereed v1 preprint posted Nov 23, 2026 without a formal Lean proof; because the Pettie–Ramachandran reduction relies on brute-force precomputation of small optimal comparison trees, the result is a foundational theoretical breakthrough rather than a drop-in practical replacement for Kruskal/Prim.

scoreRationale.foundational: Settles one of the most iconic open problems in classical graph algorithms—whether deterministic MST can run in strictly linear O(m) comparison time.
scoreRationale.ripple: Reshapes foundational algorithms curricula and demonstrates that frontier reasoning models can invent genuinely new deterministic combinatorial algorithms.
scoreRationale.verification: Carefully verified, simplified, and co-authored by leading TCS researchers (Khanna, Putterman, Song), though v1 has not yet completed conference/journal peer review.
scoreRationale.velocity: Cracked a decades-old algorithmic barrier (open since KKT 1995 / Chazelle 2000) with core ideas generated by GPT-6.2 Astra.
